newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-SEVEN WIPES SMILE FROM THE FACE OF THE TIGER.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SEVEN WIPES SMILE FROM THE FACE OF THE TIGER.

text.p: Tiger Woods rarely shows any emotion on the golf course but he gave a broad smile as a passing train hooted a salute as he was about to tee up on the 11th hole in the British Open on Thursday.
He was not smiling 463 yards later with a triple bogey seven on his card and a round turned from one-under par to two over.
The 21-year-old American did not blame the train driver. He had heard the loco coming, stepped back from his ball and waved in return salute.
But when he did tee off he pushed his drive right, almost out of bounds, and the ball nestled unplayably in a gorse bush.
Forced to take a drop, he still had a difficult lie in the rough and his two iron caught a ridge and went only about 100 yards before disappearing in tall grass.
His next shot went 120 yards and through the green, the chip back was four feet past, and he two putted.
Woods' hopes of a flying start dimmed further two holes later when he dropped another shot. He pulled his approach wide of the 13th green, chipped 18 feet past the hole and again two putted.
But the world number one refused to concede defeat to the stiff wind and the demanding back nine.

Using a two-iron from the tee on the par five 542-yard 16th into the face of the wind and again from the middle of the fairway, he left himself just a wedge shot short of the green and subsequently holed the 12-foot birdie putt.

He parred 17 and then treated the large gallery around the 18th to an outrageous recovery after pulling his tee shot into the left rough. He gave the ball a real whack with a four iron, it pitched in front of the green, hopped over the bunker and finished 18 feet from the hole.
The crowd roared with delight as the putt was duly dispatched and Woods was right back in contention again with a one-over-par 72, five off the pace.
He was certainly content afterwards. "Overall I feel pretty good in today's conditions, especially with a seven," he said.
"When you play in any kind of wind like this, it's going to be hard work. You have got to scramble and hang in there, and you have got to be very patient."

Woods was given a generous ovation as he strode on to the first tee, dapper in white sweater and shirt, blue trousers and cap. A large crowd reminiscent of 'Arnie's Army' that used to follow Arnold Palmer followed his every step.

They were treated to a ragged opening as the young American drove into a bunker and he followed by firing his ball out across the green and straight into another. However, his second sand shot was a beauty leaving him a short putt to earn an unlikely par.

His prodigious driving was soon on show. On the 557-yard par five fourth, with the wind behind him, he produced a massive drive, the ball bouncing and then rolling, rolling, rolling, finally finishing 435 yards down the centre of the fairway. His playing partners, Bernhard Langer and Steve Elkington were left more than 120 yards behind.
That huge drive almost gave him an eagle but his putt lipped the hole and he to settle for his first birdie of the round.
He said later he once drove nearly 500 yards, but added disarmingly: "In Denver, at altitude, so it doesn't count."
Another huge drive came on the 402-yard seventh when his tee shot ended in a bunker on the front edge of the green but he two-putted and had to settle for a par.
His other birdie on the front nine came at the 577-yard par five sixth where a driver and a five iron left him awkwardly on a steep downslope at the side of the green.
But showing there is far more to his game than sheer power, Woods gently chipped the ball to within two feet and holed the putt.

His first dropped shot was at the 126-yard eighth, known as the Postage Stamp and the shortest hole in championship golf. But it is far from being one of the easiest, defended by a number of deep, straight-sided bunkers.
Woods found one on the left, splashed out to six feet from the hole but missed the putt.
After his finishing birdie the Masters champion had a message for those speculating that Scotland's harsh weather would find holes in his game.

He said he hoped the wind would continue for the rest of the tournament. "When the wind is up like this, if you go out and play a good solid round and you shoot something in the 60s, let's say a low round like 67, you're going to pick up a lot of ground and a lot of shots on the field," he said.
The field has been warned.
